topics.title: Business finance and classification of sources

learn.hook: Before a single machine runs or a single shirt is sold, a business needs money. Where it gets that money from shapes its risk, control and cost.
points: Business finance means the funds required for carrying out business activities. Fixed capital requirements are funds for fixed assets (land, building, machinery); working capital requirements are funds for day-to-day operations (raw materials, wages, rent).

By period: long-term sources (more than 5 years), e.g. equity shares, preference shares, debentures, long-term loans from financial institutions; medium-term (more than 1 year but less than 5 years), e.g. bank loans, public deposits, lease financing; short-term (less than 1 year), e.g. trade credit, short-term bank loans, commercial paper.

By ownership: owners' funds (provided by the owners, e.g. equity shares and retained earnings; permanent, no fixed return, owners get control) vs borrowed funds (raised as loans, e.g. debentures, bank loans, public deposits, trade credit; for a fixed period, fixed interest, often secured by assets, no control to lenders).

By source of generation: internal sources (generated within the business, e.g. retained earnings, collection of receivables, disposing of surplus inventory) vs external sources (raised from outside, e.g. shares, debentures, loans, trade credit, public deposits).

example.q: Classify retained earnings on all three bases: period, ownership and source of generation.
steps: Period: it is a permanent, long-term source.
Ownership: profits belong to the owners, so it is owners' funds.
Generation: it comes from within the business, so it is internal.

learn.hook: When you buy one share of a listed company, you become a part-owner. You may vote at its meetings, and you get what is left after everyone else is paid.
points: Equity shares are the most important source of raising long-term capital. Equity shareholders are the owners of the company; equity is also called 'ownership capital' or 'owners' funds'. They bear the highest risk.

Rights: voting rights (they elect directors and decide policies); right to a share in residual income and assets (paid after preference shareholders and creditors); pre-emptive right (to be offered new shares first, as 'right shares').

Merits: suitable for investors willing to take risk for higher returns; no burden on the company to pay a fixed dividend; permanent capital, repayable only on winding up; provides credibility and a base for borrowing; no charge on assets; democratic control through voting.

Limitations: investors who want steady income may not prefer them; cost of equity is higher (dividends are not tax-deductible, and issue costs are high); issue of more equity can dilute voting power of existing shareholders; more formalities and delays.

example.q: A company has a profit of ₹10,00,000 to distribute. It must first pay ₹2,00,000 as preference dividend. It has 1,00,000 equity shares. If the whole remainder is distributed, what is the dividend per equity share?
steps: Dividend per share = 8,00,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹8.

learn.hook: Preference shareholders are like passengers with priority boarding: they get their dividend and their capital back before equity shareholders, but they usually cannot steer the plane.
points: Preference shares carry two preferential rights over equity shares: (i) to receive a fixed rate of dividend out of profits before equity holders, and (ii) to receive repayment of capital before equity holders on winding up. They generally have no voting rights except on matters affecting their own rights.

Merits: steady income for investors who want safety; no dilution of control; no charge on assets; fixed dividend lets equity holders earn more when profits are high (trading on equity); preference in liquidation.

Limitations: not suitable for investors willing to take risk; reduces equity holders' claims on assets; rate of dividend is usually higher than debenture interest; dividend is not tax-deductible, so they are costlier than debt.

Types: cumulative (unpaid dividend accumulates and is paid in later profitable years) vs non-cumulative (arrears lapse); participating (share in surplus profits after equity dividend) vs non-participating; convertible (can be converted into equity) vs non-convertible.
Equity vs preference: dividend fluctuating vs fixed; paid last vs before equity; full voting vs limited voting; higher risk vs lower risk; capital repaid last vs before equity.

example.q: A company has ₹5,00,000 of 10% cumulative preference shares. It paid no dividend for two years. In year 3, it has enough profit. How much preference dividend must it pay before any equity dividend?
steps: Annual dividend = 10% of 5,00,000 = ₹50,000.
Arrears for 2 years = ₹1,00,000, plus ₹50,000 for year 3.

learn.hook: Instead of paying out all its profit, a company can keep some of it to buy new machines. Money it doesn't have to borrow or beg for: retained earnings.
points: A company does not distribute all its profits as dividend; it keeps a part for future use. This is called retained earnings or ploughing back of profits. It is an internal source of finance, a part of owners' funds.

Merits: permanent source of funds; no explicit cost in the form of interest, dividend or issue expenses; no dilution of control; enhances the company's capacity to absorb unexpected losses; may lead to an increase in the market price of equity shares.

Limitations: excessive ploughing back may cause dissatisfaction among shareholders, as they get lower dividends; it is an uncertain source, since profits fluctuate; the opportunity cost of these funds is often not recognised, which may lead to their sub-optimal use.

learn.reallife: Many large Indian companies fund new plants largely from their own reserves, built up by years of ploughing back profits.

learn.hook: If a company sells you a '9% debenture', you are not an owner but a lender. You get 9% interest every year, profit or loss.
points: Debentures (and bonds) are instruments for raising long-term debt capital. A debenture is an acknowledgement of debt by the company; debenture holders are creditors who get a fixed rate of interest, e.g. 9% debentures pay 9% interest every year on their face value.

Merits: preferred by investors who want fixed income at lesser risk; fixed charge, so holders do not share in extra profits; no dilution of control (no voting rights); interest is a tax-deductible expense, so debt is cheaper than shares.
Limitations: fixed obligation to pay interest is a burden in lean years; the company must provide for redemption; assets may be mortgaged, reducing further borrowing capacity.

Types: secured (charge on assets) vs unsecured; registered (names recorded, transfer by a regular instrument) vs bearer (transferable by delivery); convertible (into equity) vs non-convertible; first (repaid before second) vs second debentures.

Shares vs debentures: ownership capital vs borrowed capital; holders are owners vs creditors; dividend (paid only from profits) vs interest (paid even if there is a loss); voting rights vs no voting rights; no security vs usually secured; repaid after creditors vs repaid before shareholders on winding up.

example.q: A company issues 20,000 10% debentures of ₹100 each. What is the annual interest? If it is in the 30% tax bracket, how much tax does this interest save?
steps: Interest is tax-deductible: tax saved = 30% of 2,00,000 = ₹60,000.

topics.title: Loans from commercial banks and financial institutions

learn.hook: A small firm needs ₹10 lakh for three years for new machines; a big firm needs ₹500 crore for fifteen years for a new plant. They usually knock on different doors.
points: Commercial banks give loans for fixed periods, cash credit, overdrafts and other facilities, usually for short and medium terms, and generally against security.

Merits of bank loans: timely financial assistance; secrecy is maintained (no public disclosure needed); an easier source as no prospectus or issue formalities are needed; flexible, since the loan can be increased or repaid early.

Limitations of bank loans: generally for short periods, and extension or renewal is uncertain; detailed investigation and securities or personal guarantees are needed; banks may impose restrictive terms, e.g. on sale of mortgaged goods.

Financial institutions (such as IFCI, the State Financial Corporations and, historically, ICICI and IDBI) were set up by the central and state governments to give long and medium-term finance, especially for expansion and modernisation.

Merits of FI loans: long-term finance not available from banks; financial, managerial and technical advice; loan obtained increases goodwill; easy instalment repayment; available even during depression. Limitations: rigid criteria and lengthy formalities; restrictions on dividend payments; FIs may nominate directors to the board, restricting management freedom.

example.q: A company takes a ₹12,00,000 term loan at 10% simple interest per year, repayable at the end of 3 years. How much interest does it pay in total?
steps: Interest per year = 10% of 12,00,000 = ₹1,20,000.

points: Trade credit is the credit extended by one trader to another when goods are bought on credit without immediate payment. It appears in the buyer's books as sundry creditors or accounts payable. It is a short-term source of finance.

Merits of trade credit: a convenient and continuous source; readily available if the buyer's creditworthiness is known; promotes sales by letting buyers stock more; does not create any charge on assets.
Limitations of trade credit: easy credit may induce overtrading and add to risks; only a limited amount is available; generally costly compared with most other sources (cash discounts are lost).

Inter-corporate deposits (ICDs) are unsecured short-term deposits made by one company with another. Types: three months deposits, six months deposits, and call deposits (withdrawable by the lender on giving one day's notice).

Characteristics of ICDs: the rate of interest varies with the amount, period and creditworthiness; the ICD market is unorganised, informal and based on mutual trust; they are mainly used to meet short-term cash shortages.

example.q: A retailer buys goods worth ₹1,00,000 on 60 days' credit. The supplier offers a 2% cash discount for immediate payment. What does the retailer give up by using trade credit?

topics.title: Other sources: factoring, lease financing, public deposits and commercial paper

learn.hook: A company can rent a machine instead of buying it, sell its unpaid bills to collect cash early, or borrow from the public for a few years. Finance has many doors.
points: Factoring: a financial service in which a factor (often a bank subsidiary) buys a firm's receivables or collects them on its behalf, and may also provide credit information. Merits: cheaper than financing receivables through other sources; quick cash; no charge on assets; the firm can focus on its business. Limitations: may be costly when invoices are many and small; the factor may pressurise customers, hurting goodwill.

Lease financing: the lessor (owner) gives the lessee the right to use an asset in return for periodic lease rentals. Merits: assets can be acquired with lower investment; simple documentation; lease rentals are tax-deductible; no dilution of ownership; lessor bears the risk of obsolescence. Limitations: restrictions on use; operations may suffer if the lease is not renewed; may be costlier than buying; the lessee does not become the owner.

Public deposits: deposits raised by companies directly from the public, usually at higher interest than bank deposits, generally for medium terms. Merits: simple procedure; cost lower than bank loans; no charge on assets; no dilution of control. Limitations: new companies find it hard to raise; unreliable when large amounts are needed; collection may be difficult.

Commercial paper (CP): an unsecured promissory note issued by a firm to raise short-term funds (up to one year). Merits: sold directly to investors, no restrictive conditions; freely transferable; provides more funds than many sources; a continuous source since a maturing CP can be repaid by a fresh issue; companies can park surplus funds in CP. Limitations: only financially sound, highly rated firms can issue it; amount limited by the surplus liquidity of investors; it is an impersonal method and maturity cannot be extended.
Note: discounting of bills of exchange and international sources (ADR, GDR) were removed in rationalisation and are not covered.

example.q: A logistics firm wants 50 trucks but does not want to block ₹20 crore in buying them. It pays monthly rentals to a finance company that owns the trucks. Which source is this, and who bears obsolescence risk?
steps: Using an asset owned by another in return for rent = lease financing.
The finance company is the lessor; the logistics firm is the lessee.
The lessor bears the risk of obsolescence.
example.answer: Lease financing; the lessor bears obsolescence risk.

topics.title: Factors affecting the choice of source of funds

learn.hook: Equity, debentures, bank loan, trade credit... there is no single 'best' source. The right one depends on cost, risk, control, time and more.
points: Cost: both the cost of procurement (issue expenses) and the cost of using the funds (interest, dividend) matter. Financial strength and stability of operations: a firm with stable earnings can take on fixed-charge debt; an unstable one should prefer owners' funds.

Form of organisation and legal status: a sole trader or partnership cannot issue shares; companies can. Purpose and time period: long-term needs (fixed assets) should be met by long-term sources; short-term needs (working capital) by short-term sources.

Risk profile: equity is the least risky for the company (no fixed obligation); debt is riskier (fixed interest and repayment). Control: issuing equity can dilute control; debt and preference shares do not.

Effect on creditworthiness: heavy secured debt may reduce the firm's ability to borrow further and its credit standing. Flexibility and ease: restrictive conditions of some lenders reduce flexibility.
Tax benefits: interest on debentures and loans is tax-deductible, while dividends on shares are not, so debt is tax-efficient.

example.q: The founders of a company want to raise ₹10 crore for expansion without losing control. Profits are stable. Which source suits them, and on which factors?
steps: They want no dilution of control, so avoid new equity.
Stable profits mean they can bear fixed interest.
Interest is tax-deductible.
So debentures or a long-term loan suit them.
example.answer: Debentures or long-term loans, based on control, financial stability and tax benefit.
